voice_profile: Mature British male medical lecturer. Deep, warm, calm and intelligent. Speak like a senior clinician teaching beside an interactive physiology diagram. Do not read the visible text verbatim. Refer naturally to what is appearing on screen, then add the physiological connection or clinical insight that makes it memorable. Natural pauses. Restrained authority. No theatrical delivery, advertising tone, sighing, breathiness or vocal fry. Clear UK pronunciation.

stages.script: Here we have Maya, twelve years old. Three weeks of thirst, polyuria and weight loss, and now abdominal pain, vomiting and unusually deep breathing. Her pulse is 128 and respiratory rate 32. She is dry, but alert and afebrile. Before naming the diagnosis, look for a single physiological disturbance that could connect the whole story. The chronic symptoms tell us this started well before today. The breathing tells us the body is now compensating for something important. Keep those two timescales in mind.

DKA is the best unifying diagnosis, but don't move on just because you recognised it. Ask what that diagnosis now has to prove. It must explain why glucose is accumulating in blood while the child is losing weight. It must explain why glucose in the urine causes profound water loss. It must explain why fat suddenly becomes an emergency fuel and why that produces an acidosis. And finally it must explain why the lungs respond to a metabolic problem. That is the reasoning chain we are going to build.

Look at the normal system on the screen. The useful way to think about insulin is not simply as a glucose-lowering hormone. Think of it as the body's fed-state signal: fuel has arrived, use it and store it. Muscle takes up glucose and makes glycogen. The liver stops manufacturing glucose and favours storage. Adipose tissue receives an equally important instruction: stop releasing fat. That last action is crucial for understanding DKA. Insulin is therefore coordinating carbohydrate and fat metabolism simultaneously. When we remove insulin in the next step, watch what happens to both sides of this map.

Now remove insulin and follow the split on the diagram. On the glucose side, peripheral utilisation falls while the liver continues glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis. Blood glucose rises. Eventually the filtered glucose load exceeds renal reabsorptive capacity, glucose remains in the tubular fluid and water follows it: osmotic diuresis. On the other side, loss of insulin's restraint on hormone-sensitive lipase releases free fatty acids. The liver converts these through beta oxidation into acetyl-CoA and then ketone bodies, especially beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate. These acids consume bicarbonate. So one missing signal creates two linked emergencies: a glucose-volume problem and a fat-acid problem. That is the central picture to keep throughout the lesson.

Now use the mechanism map rather than a symptom list. Start with polyuria. Hyperglycaemia becomes glycosuria, glycosuria retains water in the tubular lumen, and the resulting osmotic diuresis produces large urinary water and electrolyte losses. Thirst is therefore not a separate feature; it is a response to that loss and the altered effective osmolality. Weight loss comes from dehydration, urinary calorie loss and a catabolic state in which fat and protein are being mobilised. Vomiting and abdominal pain sit mainly downstream of ketosis, acidaemia and dehydration. If you can travel backwards from each symptom to the map, you no longer need to memorise the classic presentation as a disconnected list.

The tachycardia belongs naturally on the volume-loss pathway: reduced effective circulating volume provokes sympathetic compensation. Now follow the acid pathway to the lungs. Ketoacids consume bicarbonate and pH falls. The respiratory system cannot excrete those ketoacids, but it can reduce carbon dioxide. Chemoreceptor-driven ventilation increases, PaCO2 falls and this partially defends pH through the bicarbonate buffer system. That is Kussmaul respiration. So when you see this deep breathing, don't think first of primary lung disease. Ask whether you are watching appropriate respiratory compensation for a metabolic acidosis.

Each investigation should now attach to a point on the map. Glucose asks whether carbohydrate regulation has failed. Blood beta-hydroxybutyrate asks whether uncontrolled fat metabolism and ketogenesis are active. Venous pH and bicarbonate ask what those ketoacids have done to acid-base balance. Then sodium, potassium, urea and creatinine tell us about the consequences of osmotic diuresis, water shifts and renal perfusion. Pay particular attention to potassium. A serum potassium of 4.7 can look reassuring while total-body stores are substantially depleted through urinary losses. Insulin deficiency, hyperosmolality and acidaemia can keep potassium extracellular. Once insulin is given, potassium moves back into cells and the hidden deficit can become obvious. Plasma concentration is not the same thing as total-body content.

Now run the physiology in reverse. Fluids address the volume pathway: restore effective circulation and renal perfusion and replace the water deficit in a controlled way. Insulin attacks the central metabolic failure. Its essential job is not merely to lower glucose; it restores the missing fed-state signal, suppresses lipolysis and switches off hepatic ketogenesis. Potassium must be anticipated because whole-body stores are depleted and insulin drives potassium intracellularly. Then comes the apparent paradox. Glucose may normalise before the ketones and acidosis have resolved. At that point dextrose may be added so that insulin can safely continue. We are sometimes giving glucose precisely so that we can keep giving the insulin needed to stop ketogenesis. Exact fluids, insulin, potassium and monitoring should follow the current paediatric DKA pathway.

Now test whether the mechanism has transferred. This child has a pump interruption, vomiting and deep breathing, but the glucose is only 14.2. If your mental definition of DKA is simply very high glucose, that number may falsely reassure you. Instead look at the other branch of the map: ketones are 4.8 and the venous pH is 7.19. Insulin-deficient ketogenesis is clearly active and it has produced metabolic acidosis. The lesson is that glucose, ketones and pH answer different physiological questions. DKA is fundamentally an insulin-deficient ketotic acidosis, not a competition to see how high the glucose can become.

Finish by rebuilding Maya without looking for a memorised list. Loss of insulin removes the fed-state signal. The liver produces glucose while peripheral utilisation falls, producing hyperglycaemia. Glycosuria then drives osmotic diuresis, explaining polyuria, thirst, dehydration and tachycardia. Simultaneously, loss of insulin's inhibition of lipolysis sends free fatty acids to the liver, ketones accumulate, bicarbonate falls and metabolic acidosis develops. Kussmaul ventilation lowers carbon dioxide to partially defend pH. Our tests measure those processes, and treatment reverses them: restore volume, give insulin until ketogenesis resolves, anticipate potassium depletion and shifts, and add dextrose when necessary so insulin can continue safely. If you can explain that causal chain, you understand DKA rather than simply remembering its algorithm.
